facts.title: Born in a German Lab
facts.text: Bohrium was first created in 1981 at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany, by a team led by Peter Armbruster and Gottfried Münzenberg. They fused chromium-54 ions into a bismuth-209 target, producing a single atom of bohrium-262. The same lab also discovered elements like hassium, meitnerium, darmstadtium, and roentgenium.

facts.title: Named for a Quantum Pioneer
facts.text: The element honors Danish physicist Niels Bohr, whose 1913 model of the atom introduced quantized electron orbits and earned him the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics. The name was formally approved by IUPAC in 1997 after a long naming dispute over several heavy elements. Its earlier placeholder name was 'unnilseptium', literally Latin-Greek for 'one-zero-seven'.

facts.title: It Vanishes in Seconds
facts.text: Every isotope of bohrium is intensely radioactive and exists only fleetingly. The most stable known isotope, bohrium-270, has a half-life of roughly 61 seconds, while many others decay in mere milliseconds. This means no measurable quantity of bohrium has ever been accumulated; it is studied one atom at a time.

facts.title: A Single Atom Chemistry Experiment
facts.text: In 2000, scientists performed actual chemistry on just six atoms of bohrium-267, forming the volatile compound bohrium oxychloride (BhO3Cl). This remarkable feat showed bohrium behaves as a Group 7 element, chemically resembling its lighter cousins technetium and rhenium. It stands as one of the most extreme examples of doing chemistry with almost nothing.

facts.title: Sits Beneath Rhenium
facts.text: On the periodic table, bohrium occupies Group 7, directly below manganese, technetium, and rhenium. Theory predicts its outer electron configuration ends in 6d5 7s2, fitting the transition-metal pattern. Its measured volatility was actually lower than rhenium's, matching predictions that periodic trends still hold even for superheavy elements.

facts.title: Made by Smashing Nuclei
facts.text: Bohrium can only be produced in particle accelerators through 'cold fusion' reactions, where a beam of medium-weight ions is fired at a heavy target nucleus. The fused nucleus must shed energy by emitting a neutron to survive, and successful events are extraordinarily rare. Detectors then identify bohrium by tracking its chain of alpha-particle decays.

facts.title: Decays in a Domino Chain
facts.text: Bohrium isotopes mostly disappear through alpha decay, ejecting helium nuclei and transforming step by step into lighter elements such as dubnium and lawrencium. Scientists confirm a bohrium atom existed by reading this signature 'decay chain' backward. Some heavier isotopes can also break apart through spontaneous fission.

facts.title: A Predicted Dense Metal
facts.text: Although no one has ever held bohrium, calculations estimate it would be a solid metal with an astonishing density near 37 grams per cubic centimeter. That would make it almost twice as dense as lead and among the densest substances ever predicted. Its appearance, likely silvery, remains purely theoretical since a visible sample will probably never exist.

facts.title: Absent From the Natural World
facts.text: Bohrium is entirely synthetic and has never been found on Earth or detected anywhere in the cosmos. Because its isotopes decay so quickly, any bohrium forged in ancient stars or supernovae would have vanished billions of years ago. It belongs to the family of elements that exist only because humans deliberately build them.

facts.title: A Member of the Superheavies
facts.text: With 107 protons, bohrium sits deep in the 'superheavy' region of the periodic table, where atomic nuclei are pushed toward the limits of stability. Studying it helps physicists test the theory of the 'island of stability', a predicted zone where certain superheavy nuclei might last far longer. Bohrium has no biological role and no commercial use, serving purely as a frontier of fundamental science.
